contraindications: Oxcarbazepine and eslicarbazepine cause dose-related hyponatremia; avoid in a patient with hyponatremia.
interactions: Carbamazepine + apixaban: strong CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein induction lowers apixaban exposure and its anticoagulant effect; avoid the combination. Induction wanes over about 2 weeks after carbamazepine is stopped.
Carbamazepine + sertraline: both cause SIADH (additive hyponatremia); carbamazepine also induces sertraline metabolism; monitor sodium.
Carbamazepine + atorvastatin: CYP3A4 induction lowers atorvastatin exposure.
Fosphenytoin or phenytoin + apixaban: CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein induction lowers apixaban exposure; avoid the combination.
Fosphenytoin + metoprolol: additive bradycardia and hypotension during IV loading; continuous ECG and blood pressure monitoring.
Lacosamide + metoprolol: additive PR prolongation and bradycardia; risk of AV block; obtain an ECG before loading.
Valproate + aspirin: aspirin displaces valproate from albumin (higher free fraction) and both impair platelet function; additive bleeding risk with apixaban.

Levetiracetam + apixaban, metoprolol, sertraline or atorvastatin: no clinically relevant pharmacokinetic interaction; levetiracetam is renally cleared, so reduce the maintenance dose for creatinine clearance 30-50 mL/min.
output.proposed: Lorazepam and a second-line antiseizure medication (levetiracetam, fosphenytoin, valproate or lacosamide) in place of carbamazepine, with apixaban, metoprolol, lisinopril, metformin, atorvastatin, aspirin and sertraline

output.query: Hyponatremia with seizures: hypertonic saline and correction limits; antiseizure drugs causing SIADH

results.finding: Severely symptomatic hyponatremia, including seizures, is treated with 150 mL of 3% saline over 20 minutes, repeated up to twice while checking sodium, aiming for a 5 mmol/L rise in the first hour.
The rise in serum sodium should not exceed 10 mmol/L in the first 24 hours and 8 mmol/L in each further 24 hours.
Patients at high risk of osmotic demyelination (alcohol misuse, malnutrition, hypokalemia, liver disease, sodium 105 mmol/L or below) should have a correction of at most 8 mmol/L in 24 hours.

SIADH is diagnosed with hypotonic hyponatremia, inappropriately concentrated urine and urine sodium above 30 mmol/L in a euvolemic patient with normal thyroid and adrenal function; carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine and SSRIs are common drug causes.

output.summary: Hyponatremia with seizures is treated with bolus 3% saline aiming for a 5 mmol/L rise in the first hour, without exceeding 10 mmol/L in the first 24 hours and 8 mmol/L in each further 24 hours [Spasovski_2014]; high-risk patients are limited to 8 mmol/L in 24 hours [Verbalis_2013]. SIADH is a diagnosis of hypotonic, euvolemic hyponatremia with concentrated urine, and antiseizure drugs and SSRIs are frequent causes [Verbalis_2013].

action_criteria.rationale: Carbamazepine lowers apixaban exposure and adds to the SIADH risk of sertraline; the replacement ASM must avoid induction, hyponatremia and conduction effects with metoprolol, and be dosed for his CKD [ESETT_2019; Verbalis_2013].

prohibited_recommendations: Do NOT raise sodium by more than 10 mmol/L in the first 24 hours or 8 mmol/L in any further 24 hours: risk of osmotic demyelination syndrome
Do NOT continue carbamazepine when it is the SIADH driver
Do NOT replace carbamazepine with oxcarbazepine or eslicarbazepine, which also cause hyponatremia
Do NOT hold apixaban without reviewing thromboembolic risk: discuss with neurology and hematology
required_recommendations: Give a benzodiazepine now: IV lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg (maximum 4 mg per dose, repeat once), or IM midazolam 10 mg without IV access [Glauser_2016].

Treat the seizure-associated hyponatremia with 150 mL of 3% saline over 20 minutes, repeated up to twice while checking sodium, aiming for a rise of 5 mmol/L in the first hour; do not exceed 10 mmol/L in the first 24 hours and 8 mmol/L in each further 24 hours; then fluid restriction for SIADH [Spasovski_2014; Verbalis_2013].

Load a second-line ASM: levetiracetam 60 mg/kg IV (maximum 4500 mg), with the maintenance dose reduced for his CKD, and avoid fosphenytoin because, like carbamazepine, it induces apixaban metabolism and adds bradycardia and hypotension with metoprolol [ESETT_2019].
Stop carbamazepine, the SIADH driver with a level of 14.2 mcg/mL, once levetiracetam is loaded, and review sertraline, which also causes SIADH.
Continue video-EEG for at least 24 hours after clinical and electrographic seizure control [Brophy_2012].
Continue apixaban at 5 mg twice daily (he meets only the creatinine criterion for dose reduction); its effect recovers as carbamazepine induction wanes.

avoided_actions.rationale: No new cardiac question: atrial fibrillation is known and anticoagulated, and no new embolic event is present.
Known rate-controlled atrial fibrillation; ICU telemetry covers rhythm monitoring and a Holter adds nothing to SE management.
Amyloid PET has no role in acute SE evaluation; dementia biomarker imaging does not change acute management.
Carotid duplex is for ischemic stroke workup; SE without focal vascular suspicion does not warrant carotid imaging.
Polysomnography studies sleep disorders and has no role in the acute evaluation of status epilepticus.

key_clinical_evidence: Carbamazepine is a classic cause of SIADH; a dose increase in a chronic CBZ user can produce hyponatremia (Na 123) that precipitates SE
Chronic structural focus (post-stroke epilepsy) lowers the threshold so a metabolic perturbation precipitates SE
Sodium correction must not exceed 10 mmol/L in the first 24 hours and 8 mmol/L in each further 24 hours [Spasovski_2014]
Carbamazepine and phenytoin induce apixaban metabolism; the replacement ASM should be non-inducing

patient.history_present_illness: A 71-year-old African American male was transferred from a skilled nursing facility to the emergency department after nursing staff found him minimally responsive in his bed during morning rounds. A nursing aide reported witnessing him shake briefly — 'his whole body was stiff and then rhythmically jerking' — for about 90 seconds approximately 2 hours before presentation. He was incontinent of urine during the episode. After the shaking stopped, he did not return to his baseline. He is a nursing home resident with moderate vascular dementia, prior stroke, and multiple medical comorbidities. At baseline per staff, he speaks in short sentences, recognizes his daughter, and follows simple commands. On arrival to the ED he is awake with eyes open but stares blankly, does not respond to his name, and produces only incomprehensible sounds. His carbamazepine was recently increased 3 weeks ago from 200 mg BID to 400 mg BID for worsening behavioral symptoms attributed to frontal lobe seizures. His daughter states his confusion seems different from his usual post-seizure state — 'He usually comes back within 20 minutes. It's been hours now.'
